name: Tool Index
tagline: A public directory where makers list their software tools so other people can find them.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software here is trivial: a list of tools, tags, a search box, a submission form. An agent can produce that in an afternoon and it will look fine. What it cannot produce is anyone arriving at it, which is the entire product, because people list on a directory for the traffic and the backlink, not for the CRUD. Your self-hosted clone is a directory of one with zero visitors, and a directory with zero visitors is a spreadsheet with worse ergonomics. The only version of this worth building for yourself is a private index of tools you actually use.
coreLoopDIY: Builds a static, searchable, self-hosted index of tools you personally track, with per-tool notes and an RSS feed of new additions.
requirements: Any static host or just a local preview server
Willingness to write your own entries, since nobody will submit to you
whatYouLose: The audience: the traffic that makes a public listing worth anything
Whatever search authority the domain has accumulated, which is the actual product being sold
Inbound submissions, so your index only ever contains what you type into it
Curation and moderation done by someone else, including spam and dead-link cleanup
Being discoverable by people who have never heard of you
moatNotes: Directories are a two-sided traffic business wearing a database as a costume: listers pay for visitors, visitors show up because of listings.
whyPeopleStillPay: Nobody pays a directory for its features. They pay for placement in front of an existing audience and for a link from a domain that search engines already trust. That is a distribution purchase, and distribution is the one thing a code generator cannot emit. The honest question for any tool directory is not whether you could build it but whether that particular directory sends real humans anywhere, and that is answerable with analytics rather than with an agent.
notes: The site is a weekend build; the audience is not. The moat is accumulated traffic and search authority, which is exactly what listers are buying.
prompt:
Build a personal tool index: a static, self-hosted directory of software tools I use or want to remember.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Astro with TypeScript, no UI framework, plain CSS in one global stylesheet
- Content via Astro content collections: one YAML file per tool in src/content/tools/, markdown body for notes
- Client-side search with Fuse.js as a local dependency, no CDN scripts
- Output: static files in dist/, deployable to any static host

Data model per tool: name, domain, category, tags array, priceNote (free text, never a fake number), summary (one line), status (using, trialing, dropped), dateAdded, plus the markdown body for longer notes.

Pages:
- / : all tools, newest first, with a search box and tag filter chips that filter in place without a page reload
- /t/[slug] : single tool page rendering the markdown notes
- /c/[category] : category listing
- /feed.xml : RSS of recently added tools

Also build:
- npm run add : a Node script that prompts for the fields and writes a validated YAML file with a slugified filename
- A zod schema in src/content/config.ts so the build fails loudly on bad or missing fields
- 12 seed entries so no page renders empty

Explicitly out of scope: user accounts, public submission forms, moderation queues, paid listings, analytics, telemetry, any hosted database or third-party API. No secrets are required; if you add a .env, the build must still succeed without it.

Finish with a README covering: how to add a tool, how to run dev, how to build, how to deploy dist/.
